about: Verb tables: the most important English verbs in the present simple, past simple and present perfect. Page /grammatik/verben, search hits via src/lib/verbtabellen.js. Forms in the order I, you, he/she/it, we, you (plural), they. A regular verb needs only `regular: true`; verbtabellen.js works out the rest (-s/-es/-ies, -ed/-d/-ied, doubled consonant, British -ll-). `p2` is the past participle; every perfect is have/has + p2. Group ids are kept from the German tables: hilfsverb = be/have/do, modal = modal verbs, unregelmaessig = irregular, regelmaessig = regular, trennbar = phrasal verbs (the particle comes after the verb: forms are written with it).

groups.name: be, have, do
groups.what: The three verbs English uses to build questions, negatives and tenses – and they are irregular.
regel: *be* + -ing = continuous: *I am working. She was sleeping.*
*have* + past participle = perfect: *I have finished. She had left.*
*do / does / did* makes questions and negatives in the present and past simple: *Do you like it? She doesn't work. Did you go?*
All three are also normal verbs: *I am tired. I have a car. I do my homework.*
In speech they are usually short: *I'm, she's, we've, don't, didn't.*

groups.name: Modal verbs
groups.what: They say if something is possible, necessary or allowed – always with a second verb in the base form.
meaning: strong obligation, often the speaker's own
obligation from rules or other people
regel: Modal + base form, no *to*: *I can swim.* (not *I can to swim*)
No -s with he/she/it: *she can, he must.*
No do in questions and negatives: *Can you help? You mustn't smoke here.*
Most modals have no past or participle: use *could, had to, been able to*: *I had to work yesterday.*
*mustn't* = it is not allowed; *don't have to* = it is not necessary. *You mustn't come ≠ You don't have to come.*

groups.name: Irregular verbs
groups.what: The past simple and the past participle don't end in -ed. You have to learn them.
regel: You can't see it from the base form, so learn the three forms together: *go – went – gone.*
The present simple is regular for almost all of them: *he goes, she sees, it takes.*
Past simple: one form for every person: *I went, they went.* Only *be* has two: *was / were.*
Present perfect: *have/has* + past participle: *I have seen, she has written.*
More irregular verbs, grouped by pattern: the list of regular and irregular verbs.

groups.name: Regular verbs
groups.what: Base form + -s for he/she/it, + -ed for the past. Almost all verbs work like this.
regel: Present simple: he/she/it adds *-s*: *I work, she works.* After s, sh, ch, x, o: *-es*: *he watches, she goes.*
Past simple and past participle: *-ed*: *I worked, I have worked.*
Ending in -e: only *-d*: *liked, lived.* Consonant + y: *-ies, -ied*: *studies, studied.*
One short vowel + one consonant: double it: *stop – stopped.* British English: *travel – travelled* (US: *traveled*).
New verbs are always regular: *google – googled, text – texted.*

groups.name: Phrasal verbs
groups.what: Verb + particle (up, out, back …). The verb changes; the particle stays the same: I got up at seven.
regel: Only the verb changes: *get up – gets up – got up – has got up.*
The verb keeps its own forms, regular or irregular: *wake up – woke up – woken up.*
With a pronoun object, the pronoun goes in the middle: *Pick me up. Find it out.* (not *Pick up me*)
The meaning is often not the meaning of the two parts: *find out* = discover, *pick up* = collect.
More phrasal verbs, and where the object goes: the phrasal verbs list.
